name: Kinesiology / face taping
lead: Kinesiology or face taping is the application of elastic therapeutic tape, of the kind developed for sports and musculoskeletal use, to the face. In appearance-focused communities it is described as a way to retrain facial muscles, lift or hold tissue, or reduce puffiness.

Elastic kinesiology tape was developed in the 1970s by Kenzo Kase, a Japanese-American chiropractor, and is sold under the Kinesio brand among others. Manufacturers have claimed benefits for muscle support, lymphatic drainage, pain signalling and proprioception, and published reviews of the tape in musculoskeletal conditions have reported small or inconsistent effects, with some researchers attributing reported benefits to placebo.[1]

No published study was found that tests kinesiology tape for cosmetic facial purposes. A registered trial compares a physiotherapy technique with kinesiology taping in patients with Bell's palsy, a medical condition.[2]

paras: Kinesiology tape is a thin, stretchy, latex-free cotton strip that can stretch to roughly 140% of its length and bonds with a heat-activated acrylic adhesive. On the body it may be worn for several days.[1]

Manufacturers state that the tape supports muscles, tendons, ligaments and joints, and further claims include improved lymphatic drainage, reduced pain signalling and better proprioception. Critics say these claims lack supporting evidence.[1]

A 2012 meta-analysis reported trivial pain relief and little quality evidence for the tape over other elastic taping in sports injuries. A 2014 meta-analysis reported negligible effects on muscle strength, with lower-quality studies more likely to report benefit. A 2015 meta-analysis found the tape outperformed no treatment for chronic musculoskeletal pain but not other treatments, and did not reduce disability. A 2018 study found tape colour, placement and tension did not measurably affect performance, strength or function. Some researchers attribute reported benefits to a placebo effect.[1]

The sources reviewed do not describe established protocols or outcomes for taping the facial skin for appearance. In medical settings, a registered trial (started 2025) compares Kabat rehabilitation with kinesiology taping in Bell's palsy.[2] Safety and adverse effects of facial taping, such as skin irritation from adhesive, are not covered by the sources reviewed.

No studies found for cosmetic facial taping. One registered trial in Bell's palsy patients compares Kabat rehabilitation with kinesiology taping; it was listed as active, not recruiting, with 38 participants, and no results were reviewed.[2]

timeline.event: Kenzo Kase develops elastic kinesiology tape.[1]
Meta-analyses report small or inconsistent effects in musculoskeletal conditions.[1]

card.summary: Elastic sports tape applied to the face to 'retrain' muscles; the tape's general evidence is limited and facial use is untested.
card.aka: face taping, Kinesio tape on face
card.note: No studies of cosmetic facial use found; adhesive effects on facial skin not documented in the sources reviewed.

quick.overview:
Face taping borrows elastic kinesiology tape from sports medicine and applies it to the face, with the claimed aim of retraining muscles or holding tissue.

Reviews of the tape for musculoskeletal pain and strength report small or inconsistent effects, and no study of cosmetic facial use was found.
quick.mechanism: Manufacturers say the tape supports tissue, aids lymph drainage and improves proprioception. Critics and some researchers say these mechanisms are unsupported and benefits may reflect placebo.
quick.risks: Safety for facial use is not documented in the sources reviewed. Adhesive tape in general can irritate skin.
